equations.name: Consumption in the price's volume unit

output.meaning: annual fuel consumption in the price's volume unit

terms.meaning: litres in one unit u (exact legal definitions)

equations.explanation: An explicit unit conversion. The factor is exact (barrel → gallon = 42) or correctly rounded to 34 significant digits (kilolitre → gallon).

equations.name: Baseline benchmark fuel cost in US dollars

terms.meaning: annual consumption in the price's volume unit

equations.explanation: What the year's fuel costs at the benchmark price.

assumptions.text: The fuel bill is consumption × the benchmark jet fuel price × the exchange rate. Taxes, fees and supplier margins that do not follow the benchmark are outside the model.

limitations.text: Only the benchmark-linked fuel cost is modelled. Ad-valorem taxes that scale with the price are not captured, so a real fuel bill can move more than the benchmark.

equations.name: Baseline benchmark fuel cost in the reporting currency
equations.explanation: An explicit currency conversion at the baseline exchange rate (an input, never assumed).

assumptions.text: The exchange rate affects the fuel bill only: other dollar costs and any dollar revenue are outside the model.

equations.name: Fuel share of operating costs

output.meaning: benchmark fuel cost as a share of operating costs

equations.explanation: A consistency check: the fuel bill cannot exceed operating costs (f ≤ 1).

equations.name: Monthly baseline fuel cost

output.meaning: baseline fuel cost in one month

equations.explanation: A frequency conversion: an annual flow spread evenly over twelve months.

assumptions.text: Fuel is consumed evenly through the year: each month uses one twelfth of the annual volume, and annual revenue and costs accrue evenly.

limitations.text: Monthly steps: timing within a month is ignored, and seasonality is not modelled.

equations.name: Jet fuel log-change

output.meaning: log-change of the jet fuel price in month m

equations.explanation: Propagated by the transmission engine along rule T1 (Brent crude → influences → jet fuel), plus the direct change to jet fuel itself.

assumptions.text: Scenario changes are permanent step changes that start in month 1 and last for the whole horizon.
Jet fuel responds to crude oil with a constant elasticity β after a lag: ln(jet fuel) changes by β × ln(1 + crude change). With β = 1 the refining margin stays a constant proportion of the price.

limitations.text: The elasticity, lags, hedge terms and pass-through are assumptions with stated defaults. None has been estimated from data in RUMIN.

equations.name: Jet fuel price relative to baseline

output.meaning: jet fuel price in month m relative to the baseline

terms.meaning: log-change of the jet fuel price

equations.explanation: Turns the log-change back into a price ratio (r = 1.3 means +30 %).

equations.name: Exchange rate relative to baseline

output.meaning: exchange rate relative to the baseline

equations.explanation: The reporting currency's price of a dollar, relative to the baseline.

assumptions.text: Scenario changes are permanent step changes that start in month 1 and last for the whole horizon.
The exchange rate affects the fuel bill only: other dollar costs and any dollar revenue are outside the model.

equations.name: Hedged share in month m
equations.formula: h(m) = h if m ≤ M_h, otherwise 0

output.meaning: share of month m's fuel that is hedged

equations.explanation: Hedges cover the first M_h months and are not rolled over.

assumptions.text: Hedged fuel pays the baseline US-dollar price until the hedges expire; the exchange rate is not hedged; hedges are not rolled over.

equations.name: Scenario monthly fuel cost

output.meaning: fuel cost in month m under the scenario

terms.meaning: jet fuel price relative to baseline

equations.explanation: Hedged fuel keeps the baseline dollar price; unhedged fuel pays the new price. All fuel is paid in dollars converted at the new exchange rate.

assumptions.text: Everything the model does not include stays at its baseline: fuel consumption, other costs, traffic, capacity, fares (apart from the stated pass-through) and financing.
The fuel bill is consumption × the benchmark jet fuel price × the exchange rate. Taxes, fees and supplier margins that do not follow the benchmark are outside the model.
Hedged fuel pays the baseline US-dollar price until the hedges expire; the exchange rate is not hedged; hedges are not rolled over.
The exchange rate affects the fuel bill only: other dollar costs and any dollar revenue are outside the model.

equations.name: Change in fuel cost

output.meaning: change in fuel cost in month m

equations.explanation: Positive means the scenario costs more than the baseline.

equations.name: Fare recovery
equations.formula: Δr(m) = φ × Δb(m − L_f) if m > L_f, otherwise 0

output.meaning: change in revenue from fares in month m

equations.explanation: Fares recover a share of the change in fuel cost after a delay, for rises and falls alike.

assumptions.text: Fares recover a fixed share of the change in fuel cost after a lag, for rises and falls alike, and passenger demand does not respond.

limitations.text: Passenger demand, capacity and schedules do not respond to fares or costs.
Competitors' responses and market share are not modelled.

equations.name: Change in operating profit

output.meaning: change in operating profit in month m

equations.explanation: Everything else is held at its baseline.

assumptions.text: Everything the model does not include stays at its baseline: fuel consumption, other costs, traffic, capacity, fares (apart from the stated pass-through) and financing.

limitations.text: Operating profit only: no interest, tax, hedge accounting, working capital or cash-flow timing.

equations.name: Totals over the horizon
equations.formula: ΣΔb = Σₘ Δb(m); ΣΔr = Σₘ Δr(m); ΣΔπ = Σₘ Δπ(m), m = 1…H

output.meaning: change in operating profit over the horizon

equations.name: Operating profit over the horizon
equations.formula: Π₀ = (R − O) × H / 12; Π₁ = Π₀ + ΣΔπ

output.meaning: operating profit over the horizon under the scenario

terms.meaning: change in operating profit over the horizon

equations.explanation: The baseline is the entered annual figures, spread evenly over the horizon.

assumptions.text: Everything the model does not include stays at its baseline: fuel consumption, other costs, traffic, capacity, fares (apart from the stated pass-through) and financing.
Fuel is consumed evenly through the year: each month uses one twelfth of the annual volume, and annual revenue and costs accrue evenly.

equations.name: Operating margins
equations.formula: μ₀ = (R − O) / R; μ₁ = (R·H/12 + ΣΔr − O·H/12 − ΣΔb) / (R·H/12 + ΣΔr)

output.meaning: operating margin over the horizon under the scenario

terms.meaning: change in fuel cost over the horizon

equations.explanation: Operating profit divided by revenue, before and after the scenario.

equations.name: Steady-state annual effect

output.meaning: annual change in fuel cost once lags have passed and hedges expired

equations.explanation: The full annual effect after every lag has passed and every hedge has expired.

assumptions.text: Scenario changes are permanent step changes that start in month 1 and last for the whole horizon.
Jet fuel responds to crude oil with a constant elasticity β after a lag: ln(jet fuel) changes by β × ln(1 + crude change). With β = 1 the refining margin stays a constant proportion of the price.
Fares recover a fixed share of the change in fuel cost after a lag, for rises and falls alike, and passenger demand does not respond.

equations.name: Offsetting revenue change

output.meaning: revenue change over the horizon that would offset the fuel-cost change

terms.meaning: change in fuel cost over the horizon

equations.explanation: How much revenue would have to change, uniformly, to leave operating profit unchanged. It is arithmetic, not a recommendation to raise fares.

limitations.text: Passenger demand, capacity and schedules do not respond to fares or costs.

equations.name: Hedging effect
equations.formula: G = Σₘ b₀ × (q × r(m) − 1); hedging effect = ΣΔb − G

output.meaning: how much the hedges change the fuel-cost change

terms.meaning: jet fuel price relative to baseline
change in fuel cost over the horizon

equations.explanation: G is the change the fuel bill would see with no hedges. The bridge −G − hedging effect + ΣΔr = ΣΔπ is exact.

assumptions.text: Hedged fuel pays the baseline US-dollar price until the hedges expire; the exchange rate is not hedged; hedges are not rolled over.

edge.description: A change in Brent crude reaches the jet fuel price with elasticity β after the stated lag.

contributions.label: Change in fuel cost without hedges (horizon)

parameters.label: Crude-to-jet-fuel elasticity (β)
parameters.rationale: β = 1 keeps the refining margin a constant proportion of the price, so jet fuel moves by the same percentage as crude. A neutral starting point, not an estimate: test other values with sensitivity analysis.

parameters.label: Crude-to-jet-fuel lag
parameters.rationale: 0 assumes crude changes reach jet fuel in the same month. Set it to how the airline's fuel contracts reprice.

parameters.label: Hedge ratio
parameters.rationale: 0 assumes no hedging. Enter the share of the coming months' fuel the airline has hedged.

parameters.label: Hedge cover
parameters.rationale: 0 assumes no hedge cover. Hedges are assumed not to be rolled over when they expire.

parameters.label: Fare pass-through
parameters.rationale: 0 assumes fares do not change. Enter the share of a fuel-cost change the airline expects to pass on to passengers.

parameters.label: Fare pass-through lag
parameters.rationale: 0 assumes fares adjust in the same month as the fuel cost. Enter the delay you expect.

assumptions.text: Everything the model does not include stays at its baseline: fuel consumption, other costs, traffic, capacity, fares (apart from the stated pass-through) and financing.
Fuel is consumed evenly through the year: each month uses one twelfth of the annual volume, and annual revenue and costs accrue evenly.
The fuel bill is consumption × the benchmark jet fuel price × the exchange rate. Taxes, fees and supplier margins that do not follow the benchmark are outside the model.
Scenario changes are permanent step changes that start in month 1 and last for the whole horizon.
Jet fuel responds to crude oil with a constant elasticity β after a lag: ln(jet fuel) changes by β × ln(1 + crude change). With β = 1 the refining margin stays a constant proportion of the price.
Hedged fuel pays the baseline US-dollar price until the hedges expire; the exchange rate is not hedged; hedges are not rolled over.
Fares recover a fixed share of the change in fuel cost after a lag, for rises and falls alike, and passenger demand does not respond.
The exchange rate affects the fuel bill only: other dollar costs and any dollar revenue are outside the model.

limitations.text: The model shows the arithmetic consequence of the inputs and assumptions. It is not a forecast of what will happen, and not investment advice.
Passenger demand, capacity and schedules do not respond to fares or costs.
Competitors' responses and market share are not modelled.
Only the benchmark-linked fuel cost is modelled. Ad-valorem taxes that scale with the price are not captured, so a real fuel bill can move more than the benchmark.
The elasticity, lags, hedge terms and pass-through are assumptions with stated defaults. None has been estimated from data in RUMIN.
Monthly steps: timing within a month is ignored, and seasonality is not modelled.
Operating profit only: no interest, tax, hedge accounting, working capital or cash-flow timing.

warnings.message: Rule T1 follows a relationship the knowledge graph records as a model assumption, not an empirical finding: results that depend on it are assumption-driven.

method.contributions: Shapley values over the scenario's non-zero changes: each change is credited with its average marginal effect over every order of adding the changes. The credits add up to the total (within rounding to 10 decimal places).
method.rounding: Calculations use 34 significant digits; results are rounded half to even to 10 decimal places.
